en: An Explanation of the Eightfold Lay Disciple’s Vow.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Having paid homage to the Sugata, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the three trainings.
Setting aside the basis of the five precepts, I shall here definitively explain three types of persons: (1.a) one who practices by dwelling in seclusion from the misconduct of sensual desires.

(1.b) One is characterized by a practice of seclusion consisting merely of the restraint of sensual desires; another is characterized by a practice of seclusion consisting merely of the restraint of misconduct.
This is due to their respective prior habituation.
For one who practices the discernment of the mere desire that is difficult to abandon, conduct that is improper is impossible;
and for one who practices the discernment of the mere misconduct that is difficult to train from, conduct that is merely sensual is impossible.
It is as follows:

1. He was seen to be skilled at cutting extremely hard wood, yet lazy when it came to cutting the petals of very soft blue lotuses; 2. And though a lion cub, he possessed the prowess to approach a herd of rutting scent-elephants for battle.
Frightened by the mere movement of leaves and other things stirred by the force of a gentle breeze, deer and other animals are terrified by the sound of their own cries.
Another [type of person] is impure regarding both forms of discernment (*viveka*). With reference to the first individual (*pudgala*) therein:

Endowed with the going-forth and full ordination; beginning from the second [category], the five-limbed lay practitioner's restraint (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) has been proclaimed. With reference to the third, the *poṣadha* is mentioned.
Among these, two—the first two restraints—are to be understood in reality as pertaining to the Vinaya.
Furthermore, regarding the remaining two types of restraint, the procedure for undertaking the lay follower’s (*upāsaka*) restraint must be explained:
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels from a teacher who abides in wholesome restraint,
one undertakes [the vows] for as long as life lasts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
"And abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants. "Complete limbs" means according to the prescribed rule.

"From one who abides in the restraint" refers to one who is training in the *upāsaka*-restraint (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), and not from anyone else. "By force" means by one who is not contemptuous. "In relation to him," even though the full collection [of conditions] is present.

Because it arises from not failing in the precepts; that is, from the wholesome act of granting the restraint (*saṃvara*), and not from anything else, because a restraint whose procedure has failed is not obtained.
"Taken" means the restraint has been taken. "Going for refuge" refers to going for refuge in the Three Jewels.

It was taught first because it serves as the gateway for the undertaking of all vows. "As long as life lasts" means until the end of one's life; this is because that which is undertaken here is for the duration of one's life.
"Killing" refers to when, with the perception "I shall kill this one," one kills that very person. This is due to the [specific] cognition.
Because it is the precursor and because it is that very [act]—and not another—due to the state of being a person;
so too should it be understood below.
Theft is the taking of another's property from the presence of the owner, whether with their regard or behind their back.
Sexual misconduct is misconduct in sensual desire. By means of a part, the whole is indicated, as in the case of Satyabhāmā being called Bhāmā.
These also are fourfold: approaching one who should not be approached, approaching in an improper part of the body, and approaching in an improper place.

"Going at an improper time": these [other factors] are not mentioned here for fear of prolixity; such is the view of others. "Drinking liquor" refers to substances such as intoxicants that cause insanity.
"Abstaining from those [actions] just mentioned" refers to that which is to be abstained from.

That by which the lay practitioner's vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) is fully attained is indeed this very limb. Furthermore, the limbs consist of clarity of faith (*prasāda*). For persons lacking clarity of faith, wholesome qualities (*śubha-dharma*) do not arise.

This is just as it is said: "When seeds have been burnt by fire, there is no sprout or stalk. Because the female faculty and the male faculty are unimpaired, and because one has avoided the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth; "according to the rule" means without transgressing the prescribed method.

In this case, the procedure is as follows: one who desires the lay practitioner’s vows (upāsaka-saṃvara) should prostrate at the feet of the teacher and inform him, saying, "O Noble Son" or "Venerable Sir, please bestow upon me the lay practitioner’s vows.
Then, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, he should sit either in a squatting position or with his right knee placed on the ground.
Having placed his palms together in reverence and bowed, he shall recite the mantra and undertake [the vows], saying:
"I, so-and-so, from this day forward, with my very life, go for refuge to the Buddha.
I, so-and-so, go for refuge to the Dharma. I, so-and-so, go for refuge to the Saṅgha."
I go. Three times: I, named so-and-so, from this day forward, abstain from taking life;
likewise, I abstain from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.
Three times indeed. May the Master hold me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge three times and has undertaken the five precepts.

Thus, this fivefold set of training rules is said to constitute the complete lay practitioner's vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*). Even if one is unable to abstain from all [prohibited actions], there is great fruit for one who has definitely renounced even a single [precept] among those previously mentioned.

The *poṣadha* ceremony, which depends upon the rising of the sun, should be observed by setting aside the ornaments worn at the time of arrival. In this regard, the taking of the three refuges is as before;
this alone is the distinction. 1. Just as those noble Arhats, having abandoned the taking of life, [abstained] from the taking of life...

Abstaining from violence, having laid aside the rod and laid aside the weapon, being modest and compassionate toward all beings and living creatures— down to even an ant or a termite— I, [name], from this day forward until the rising of the sun tomorrow, shall abandon taking life and abstain from taking life. By this...

By means of the first limb, I train after them, I conform to them, and I imitate those noble Arhats: (1) just as those noble Arhats [abstained] for as long as life lasts from taking what is not given,
(2) from unchaste conduct, (3) from false speech, (4) from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis of negligence.

I, who am thus named, from this day forward until the rising of the sun at the time of death, shall likewise abstain from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of spectacles (7); from wearing garlands, scents, unguents, and cosmetics (8); and from high and luxurious beds, as well as from eating at improper times (9). I shall also abstain from taking what is not given (10) and from unchaste conduct (11).

Having abandoned false speech (5), the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants (6), the viewing of dancing, singing, music, and theatrical performances (7), the wearing of garlands, scents, unguents, and cosmetics (8), high and luxurious beds (9), and untimely eating— up to and including untimely eating— having abandoned these as well...

"I abstain from [these things]. Thus, through these eight factors, I train in accordance with the training of those noble Arhats; I conform to it; I imitate it. Three times in this manner: "May the Master consider me one who observes the *poṣadha*. Such is the restraint of the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-saṃvara*)."
Having approached the Noble Ones (*ārya*), it is called *upavāsa* because of its perfuming (*vāsanā*). It is called *poṣadha* because of the nourishing of the seeds of the wholesome (*kuśalabīja*).

By means of this undertaking of the *poṣadha*, for the sake of practicing the two kinds of seclusion (*viveka*), he will maintain steadfastness through fasting (*upavāsa*) both during the time of the fast and on the occasion of the miracle. Through gradual purification, he will [attain] this great enthusiasm.
One will undertake it for as long as life lasts.

Even though the duration is restricted to only a single day, this is due to the influence of individuals whose faculties are difficult to subdue; otherwise, the restraint would not have been taught [for such a short time]. For them as well, by means of a lifelong undertaking, there is the undertaking of the *gomi* (cowherd) restraint.

Thus it is maintained. Just like a woman or a butcher, if one is incapable of abstinence for a full day and night, one will abstain for either a single day or a single night alone. In this regard, even when "only a day" is mentioned, it is said to mean until the setting of the sun;
likewise, even when "only a night" is mentioned, it is as before. If this is the case, it constitutes merely good conduct (*sucarita*) and not the *poṣadha* vow.
Because it pertains to the duration of a day and night.

Now, in this undertaking of the lay practitioner's vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), when drinking intoxicants— which consists of the four types of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the five types of prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)— has been abandoned, how...
They have entered upon the ten paths of wholesome action. As it has been said: "One who abstains from false speech will also abstain from other faults."

"He who has desisted from false speech"—the word "that" (tat) here is used by way of referring to a single part [of the category]. He will also desist from others, namely from slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter, which are well-known faults.
The singular number is used because the desisting is from the genus of faults.

In that regard, slander (*paiśunya*) is the speaking of words that cause division among others by one with a defiled intention (*kliṣṭāśaya*). Harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) is the speaking of unpleasant words by one with precisely such a mind.
Whatever other speech involving passion and so forth there is—such as false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) and the like—by means of this very same mental state, that is [also included].
Regarding frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*):
if this is so, then only false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) was mentioned in the instruction on the training rules (*śikṣākāya*), and not slander (*paiśunya*) and the others as well.
This is because that false speech is exceedingly blameworthy; therefore, it is precisely that false speech alone [that is singled out] among all [the unwholesome vocal actions].
Because it is associated with a definitive restriction; because false speech is exceedingly censurable—false speech is indeed the most blameworthy;
because as soon as one has fallen into it, one falls into all other evils.
For a person who speaks falsely, having transgressed this one single dharma...

Because of the statement, "For one who has abandoned the next world, there is no evil that should not be committed," if this were so, how could the abstention from mental misconduct be established through the abstention from bodily and verbal misconduct?
Why? Because the abstention from unwholesome bodily and vocal actions is wholesome mental action.
From that, the abstentions from covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view are established.
Why? This has been stated immediately above: it is precisely the abstention from the misconduct of body and speech.

Regarding "wholesome action": the mind is established as having the nature of being free from attachment, aversion, and delusion, because of the statement that "all phenomena are preceded by the mind. For that very reason, by means of the partial mention of covetousness, ill-will, and [wrong] view—just as before—the whole is indicated, including wrong view. Thus, the abstentions are established; "abstentions" refers to the act of abstaining.
Because they are numerous, the abstentions are also expressed in the plural.

Among them, *abhidhyā* (covetousness) is the improper longing of one who thinks, "May that which belongs to others, such as their women or property, be mine. *Vyāpāda* (malice) is cruel thought such as, "I would kill these beings," and so forth. *Mithyādṛṣṭi* (wrong view) is as follows:
The defiled lack of wisdom (*kliṣṭadauṣprajñā*) belongs to one who denies karma, its results, and so forth.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is an eleven-limbed lay practitioner’s vow (*upāsakasaṃvara*). How then does it become five-limbed?
It is because the entry [into the vows] is intended to consist of exactly five limbs.

This is true. When the Blessed One first spoke of the "vow of the five-limbed practitioner" and so forth, his intention was that this would serve as an easy entry point for those of limited intelligence, so that they might gradually become capable of abstaining from other unwholesome actions as well.
Regarding what was said— that the Blessed One’s intention is that there is abstention from all [unwholesome actions]— in this matter, monks, or a son of good family,
or a daughter of good family, become endowed with serene confidence. They become those who exercise confidence regarding the entirety of the maturation of karma,
who reach a firm conviction, and who are free from doubt.
Having understood that the fruit of black and white karma is never lost, he does not perform an improper act even for the sake of his life.
He abstains from taking life, and he abstains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. He...
One proceeds to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action, thinking, "I shall not commit the ten unwholesome paths of action," and so forth.
In this way, the restraint of the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-saṃvara) is to be understood.
Thus, the eleven abstentions are established. [The question arises: Is the restraint present when all [the factors] are lost, or even when some are lost?
What is destroyed? Killing a human being, stealing with full intent, taking another's wife, and lying are the causes for the destruction of one's vows.

1. To cause the destruction of the life-span of human beings—whether they have five limbs fully formed, are still in the womb, or have already emerged—by means of medicine, rice, or similar substances, is the first offense.
2. The theft of a full one-fourth of a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin, or of an object of equivalent value, is [the second offense].
The second [is this].
The third is the approach to another's wife either by force or out of desire for her.
The fourth is said to be the nature of false speech, namely, the claim that one possesses knowledge of others' minds and so forth.
Does this lay follower, upon the arising of even one of the four offenses involving defeat (*patanīya-dharma*), become like a monk who has committed a defeat and is no longer a worthy vessel,
and thus fail to take the vows again in this very life? Let him take the vows again from such a person as before.

It is from such a person as previously described that [the vow] is obtained; it is not, however, by oneself, as is the case with the bodhisattva vow. It is held that the attainment of the *prātimokṣa* vow arises from the informative intimation (*vijñapti*) of another. Furthermore, one will subsequently receive the lay follower’s vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) in due order.

Now, when another rule has arisen, how should it be performed? How, then, should others be instructed? They should be instructed for the sake of what is wholesome—that is, for a person who is endowed with the power of vocal intimation and the understanding of its meaning, and who is endowed with restraint in action.

He will abandon other transgressions than those involving defeat—namely, the offenses of killing living beings, harsh speech, divisive speech, unchaste conduct, and so forth—as well as the drinking of intoxicants.
How so? ... by undertaking physical application with earnestness, in the interim...

Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, sitting in the squatting posture (uṭkuṭuka), or having placed the right knee-cap on the ground and bowed with palms joined, one should announce the matter and confess it.
This is the recitation for that confession: "May the noble son, or venerable teacher, attend to me."

"I, the lay follower named so-and-so, being possessed of the aforementioned bases of offenses, shall confess them all together in their entirety before a son of good family, an ācārya, or a bhadanta. By confessing, I shall dwell in comfort; it should not be said that I am dwelling otherwise by not confessing or failing to confess. What offense, O son of good family, do you [have]?"

"Do you see? "By this it is said: 'I see. Then he is asked again: "What will you conceal for the future? By this it is further said: "I shall conceal. He promises, saying, "Very well. "Knowing, seeing, and remembering, I shall act in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. This is repeated three times.

Since [the rules] for other minor offenses have already been established, how is this [present rule] formulated? If one asks "which are the minor ones," those which are other than the *pātayantikās*—namely, incomplete members of the [offenses] such as taking life and incomplete members of the [offenses] such as slander—are the minor ones that must be restrained; that is auspicious.

One should generate the thought: "I shall once again conceal such conduct. No confession need be made merely because it has been concealed, since one has emerged from it. Furthermore, for the sake of purifying all karmic obscurations, there is the Dharma discourse of the Three Aggregates (*triskandhaka*).
The *Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī* and [the other] should always be recited six times throughout the day and night.

Having spoken of the morality of abstention (*nivṛtti-śīla*), one honors the morality of engagement (*pravṛtti-śīla*). Thus, while established in the morality of restraint, one should honor engagement as well, according to one's capacity. In this manner, having made firm the morality of abstention through the sequence thus described, [one should practice] the morality of engagement.

Through engagement, one should honor the morality characterized by hearing, reflection, and so forth, as well as that consisting of generosity and the like, according to one's capacity, just as one would honor power.
Why is that? Because through its application, various fruits have been bestowed; that is the morality of cessation (*nivṛtti-śīla*). By means of that—
Through the application and connection of the morality of engagement (*pravṛtti-śīla*), various forms of prosperity were bestowed upon oneself.

Now, by way of conclusion, he joins one to the two kinds of morality: "In this regard, one who desires even a happy rebirth (*sugati*) must apply themselves with effort. "In this regard" means that for that reason, one must diligently practice the application of those two kinds of morality.
This is true for one who desires even a happy rebirth characterized by the excellence of gods and humans, let alone for one who desires liberation.

Now, if it is asked: "Why is it that one who has performed the two kinds of ethical discipline sometimes goes only to a miserable rebirth, and does not enter a happy rebirth despite having such a wish? [The answer is: Where has a rice seed ever been seen as the cause for a priyaṅgu sprout?
Where has it ever been seen or known that a rice seed (*śālibīja*) could serve as the cause for the sprout of a *priyaṅgu* plant?

For what reason? Because there is a fixed determination of cause and effect based on the nature of the rice seed. Likewise, it is intended [here] that since ethical discipline (*śīla*) is a cause for a happy rebirth (*sugati*), how could it possibly be a cause for birth in an evil state (*durgati*)? Such is the determination of cause and effect regarding this subject.
It is indeed the arrival of the purity of the three spheres, for there is no other means. Through the commentary on the eight points of the lay practitioner's vows revealed by me,
that which has arisen for me— possessing the power of merit— has reached as far as the path of entry into the solar vehicle.
May those beings who have entered the ocean of saṃsāra and are striving to cross over its difficult-to-traverse near and far shores,
apply themselves to the supreme enjoyment of that which is most wonderful to behold.
The Commentary on the Eight Verses on the Lay Practitioner’s Vows, composed by Ācārya Sunayaśrī, is completed.
